name: Crucible Industries Maelstrom-12 'Grinder'
description:
The Crucible Industries Maelstrom-12 is a fully automatic shotgun chambered in 12 gauge, fed from a twenty-round drum magazine, with a cyclic rate of 300 rounds per minute. The weapon features a constant-recoil operating system that spreads the recoil impulse across the entire firing cycle, making automatic fire from a 12-gauge shotgun controllable — though 'controllable' is a relative term when discussing a weapon that fires five buckshot shells per second.

The Grinder is a siege weapon in a shotgun's clothing. At room-clearing distances, a sustained burst from the Maelstrom saturates an area with buckshot pellets in a density that no individual target can survive and no group of targets can avoid. The twenty-round drum empties in four seconds of continuous fire, during which time the weapon has dispersed approximately one hundred and eighty individual buckshot pellets into the target area.

Crucible manufactures the Maelstrom-12 under exclusive contract for corponation military forces and high-tier facility defense. The weapon is not available on the civilian market at any price through legitimate channels. On the black market, Grinders command prices that rival small vehicles, and their appearance at any criminal scene triggers an immediate corponation response — the weapons are serialized, tracked, and actively hunted when they leave authorized custody.
legality: Military-restricted — unauthorized possession is a capital-class offense
specifications:
caliber: 12 gauge
effective_range: 25 meters (automatic buckshot)
rate_of_fire: Full automatic, 300 RPM
magazine_capacity: 20 rounds (drum)
weight: 5.8 kg (loaded)
tactical_use: A fully automatic shotgun for area denial and facility defense. The constant-recoil system makes sustained automatic fire controllable. The drum magazine provides twenty rounds of continuous fire capability. Devastatingly effective in confined spaces against multiple unarmored or lightly armored targets. Ammunition consumption is extreme — the weapon is logistically demanding. Not suitable for precision engagements.
cultural_context: The Grinder is a bogeyman. Most people in GLMZ have never seen one and hope they never will. Its existence represents the upper boundary of conventional weapons lethality — the point where firearms technology meets industrial-scale violence. In criminal circles, claiming to have access to a Maelstrom is either a bluff or a death wish, because corponation asset recovery teams take stolen Grinders very seriously.
story_hooks: A Grinder is used in a tunnel battle beneath the Gray Zone, and the twenty-second firefight kills more people than the district has seen die by violence in a year. The weapon is recovered — but the drum magazine has been replaced with one holding experimental ammunition.
A Crucible Industries armorer reports a Maelstrom-12 missing from inventory. The serial number doesn't match any existing weapon. Someone is manufacturing unregistered Grinders.
related_entities: Arcturus Defense Solutions Neural PDW ANPD-1 'Impulse'

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist siege weapon disguised as a shotgun — massive, angular, and purposefully intimidating. The Maelstrom-12 reads as industrial violence: a thick receiver with protruding gas tubes, a barrel shroud that dominates the silhouette, and a drum magazine that extends downward like a fuel tank. The entire profile suggests compression and controlled chaos.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 94 cm | Barrel length: 51 cm | Drum magazine diameter: 18 cm | Height with mounted optics: 32 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and front-heavy even when empty (5.8 kg loaded). The constant-recoil system distributes mass deliberately — the barrel assembly is substantial, but the receiver feels engineered for absorption rather than lightness. Not a weapon you carry one-handed for extended periods.
physical_description.primary_material: Reinforced polymer composite (receiver and handguard), chrome-moly steel barrel and gas tubes, aluminum alloy furniture
physical_description.finish: Matte battleship grey with brushed steel accents on the barrel shroud and gas system. The drum magazine is phosphate-coated steel with a slightly worn patina. Finish shows strategic wear — areas around the magazine well and grip are polished smooth from handling.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal grey primary with charcoal polymer black secondary. Crucible Industries' corporate red accent trim on the safety lever and magazine release. The drum magazine contrasts in darker steel tone.
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer pistol grip with aggressive checkering; feels designed to be held even with wet gloves or in zero-G. The fore-grip is rubberized and wrapped with tactical cord for additional purchase. Both surfaces are slightly warm to the touch from synthetic materials.
distinctive_features: Massive gas tube assembly running along the top of the barrel with visible pressure ports
Over-sized charging handle with numbered position indicator for recoil cycle phase
Twenty-round drum magazine with numbered round counter windows (1-5-10-15-20)
Integrated mounting rail system across the top and sides for optics/thermal imaging
Muzzle brake designed to cascade recoil backward along the frame axis rather than upward
Heat vents cut into the barrel shroud in diagonal patterns
Spent shell deflector angled sharply downward and forward
Crucible Industries corporate sigil stamped in red on the magazine housing
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: CRUCIBLE INDUSTRIES / MAELSTROM-12 'GRINDER' stamped into the receiver in military block font. Serial number engraved on the frame beneath the drum magazine. Contract designation 'GLMZ-DEFENSE-TIER-4' etched below the barrel. Warning labels in three languages (English, Mandarin, Spanish) on the safety mechanism.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field units show consistent wear: scuffed polymer from tactical gear contact, carbon fouling around the gas ports, cosmetic dings on the drum magazine from drum changes in the field. The finish remains intact because these weapons are maintained obsessively — they're too valuable and too tracked to allow degradation. Black carbon residue typically visible around the muzzle brake from sustained fire cycles.
